blocks.content: Have you ever tried to plug a US charger into a European socket?
Both work perfectly. They just don't fit each other. You need an adapter something that sits between them and makes them compatible without changing either side.
This is exactly what the Adapter Pattern does in code.
Your system expects one interface. The third-party library or legacy code you want to use has a completely different interface. You cannot change the library. You do not want to rewrite your system.
So you write an adapter a wrapper that translates calls from your interface into calls the other side understands.
It is useful when:
["You are integrating a legacy system or third-party library.","You want to reuse existing code without modifying it.","You need to bridge the gap between two incompatible interfaces."]

You want to reuse existing code without modifying it.
You need to bridge the gap between two incompatible interfaces.

blocks.content: No rewrites. No messy if-else checks. Just a clean wrapper that makes incompatible things work together.
Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Incompatible Logging Interfaces
Imagine you are building an application that needs a consistent logging system. Your application is designed to work with a Logger interface for handling all log messages.
The Expected Interface
Here is the contract your application expects any logger to follow:
This abstraction makes it easy to swap logging providers without changing any core business logic.
Your In-House Implementation
Your team already has an internal logger that fits this interface perfectly:
YourApplicationServiceuses this interface and works beautifully:
Here is how it gets called:
The Incompatible Third-Party Logger
Here is what that external logging class looks like:
You now have two interfaces that do the same thing but speak completely different languages:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245778856-a3b79a1a.jpg
And here is the constraint:
["You cannot change ApplicationService it is used system-wide and depends on Logger","You cannot modify ThirdPartyLogger it is from an external vendor","But you must make them work together"]
items: You cannot change ApplicationService it is used system-wide and depends on Logger
You cannot modify ThirdPartyLogger it is from an external vendor
But you must make them work together

blocks.content: What you need is a translator a class that sits between ApplicationService and ThirdPartyLogger, adapting the incompatible interface into one your system already understands.
This is exactly what the Adapter Pattern does.
2. What is the Adapter Pattern?
The Adapter Pattern acts as a bridge between two incompatible interfaces. It wraps an existing class and exposes a different interface the one the client already knows and expects.
Two things make this pattern work:

1. Translation without touching either side the adapter sits in the middle and converts calls from the client's language into the adaptee's language. Method names change. Parameters get transformed. Return types get converted. All of this happens invisibly inside the adapter.
2. Both sides stay untouched the client keeps using the interface it was built against. The adaptee keeps working exactly as it always has. The adapter is the only new piece added to the system.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245779091-d57fcfc7.png
Real-World Analogy
Think of a language interpreter at a business meeting. One person speaks English. The other speaks Japanese. Neither is willing to learn the other's language overnight.
The interpreter sits between them listening to English, translating to Japanese, and sending responses back. Both sides communicate effectively without changing how they speak.
The Adapter Pattern is that interpreter sitting between two systems that speak different languages and making sure they understand each other.
Two Ways to Build an Adapter
blocks.text: Two Ways to Build an Adapter

blocks.content: 1. Object Adapter: Composition (Recommended) The adapter holds an instance of the adaptee inside it. When a client call comes in, the adapter delegates to that instance with the necessary translation. Works in any language. Flexible and easy to maintain.

2. Class Adapter: Inheritance The adapter extends the adaptee directly and also implements the target interface. Requires multiple inheritance something Java does not support for classes. More common in C++.
In most real-world Java code, the Object Adapter is what you will use.
The Four Participants
Target Interface Logger The contract the client was built against. ApplicationService only ever calls logInfo(), logError(), and logWarning(). It has no idea what runs underneath.
Adaptee ThirdPartyLogger A perfectly capable logging library but one that speaks a completely different language. It has writeLog() and sendAlert() instead of the methods the application expects.

Adapter ThirdPartyLoggerAdapter The translator between the two worlds. It looks like a Logger to the client and acts like a ThirdPartyLogger on the inside. Every incoming call gets converted and forwarded correctly.
Client ApplicationService Calls log methods and never once suspects that a third-party library is doing the actual work. Its code has not changed by a single line.
3. How It Works
Here is the Adapter workflow step by step:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245779562-8650f0b4.png
Step 1: Client calls the Target interface ApplicationService calls logInfo(), logError(), or logWarning() on whatever Logger it was given. It has no idea what is running behind the interface.
Step 2: Adapter receives the call ThirdPartyLoggerAdapter implements Logger so it intercepts every call. It now needs to translate it into something ThirdPartyLogger understands.
Step 3: Adapter translates and delegates Each method gets mapped to the correct third-party call. Method names change. Parameters get adjusted. All of this happens invisibly inside the adapter.
Step 4: Adaptee executes ThirdPartyLogger runs its own logic completely unaware it was called through an adapter. It just sees its own methods being called normally.
Step 5: Result flows back The response travels back through the adapter to the client. ApplicationService receives the result through the Logger interface it has always known.
